title: Testing a document on someone who was not there
lead: Use it when you wrote something for people who were not in the room, because you can no longer judge your own draft: you know what every shortcut means.
produces: A document that independent readers with no context could follow, and your own record of which findings you acted on.
scenario: You drafted a one-page proposal asking the lab heads' committee to approve a four-week pilot of Run comparison v1. One committee member is a lab head from a different discipline who has never seen a reference run.
input: Here is my one-pager for the lab heads' committee. Read it cold and tell me what a stranger would not follow.

steps.label: Say who reads it and what they decide
steps.text: You write one line first: a lab head from another discipline reads this for three minutes and decides whether to approve a four-week pilot. Readers are held to that line. Without it they can only comment on style.

steps.label: A panel of fresh readers
steps.text: Three readers with no access to your notes or earlier drafts each judge the page through a different lens: a completeness checklist, a check for machine-sounding prose and a check on voice. Each scores it. Findings that two or more readers raise are fixed; one reader's finding is advice. Round one: "reference run" is never defined, "tolerance" appears as a percentage and as a count, the pilot's cost to the assay team is in the last line and nobody is named who can stop the pilot. Two or more readers raise each of those. One reader also asks for the full instrument list.

steps.label: Decide what you act on
steps.text: You act on the four shared findings: define both terms in one sentence each, move the cost to the top and name who can stop the pilot. You leave out the instrument list. Only one reader asked, and the committee decides on scope, not on hardware. You keep a note of what you changed and why; the readers' own output is their reports and scores.

steps.label: A new panel, a new context
steps.text: New readers see only the revised page. Readers who saw the first version would be checking your fixes instead of reading. This round raises one new problem: the pilot dates do not say which weeks. You fix it and call another round.

steps.label: Scores stall
steps.text: If a score gets worse after a revision, or the scores stop moving while still short of the bar, the page is probably trying to do two jobs. The method stops after four rounds whatever the scores say and hands the open findings back to you.

steps.label: Scores clear their bars
steps.text: In round three no reader's score has got worse, all three clear their bars and they barely move from the previous round. The loop worked on a local file throughout, and nothing is published or sent until this gate passes.

steps.label: The page and your record
steps.text: You have the revised one-pager and your own list of what you acted on and why. A person sends it. The method never does.

settled: "Reference run" and "tolerance" are defined where they first appear.
The pilot's cost to the assay team is in the first paragraph.
The pilot covers two of the three instruments, and the page says so.
open: Whether the committee wants the full instrument list. One reader asked twice; the other readers did not.

artifact.title: Your record (excerpt)
lines: Reader brief. A lab head from another discipline, three minutes, decides on a four-week pilot.

Round 1. Four findings raised by two or more readers, all acted on: both terms defined, cost moved to the top, owner of the stop decision named. Instrument list asked for by one reader only: not added, because the committee decides on scope.
Round 2. One new finding, pilot weeks missing: dates added.
Round 3. No score worse, all three above their bars, little movement. Ready for you to send.

stop: Stop when no reader's score has got worse, all three scores clear their bars and they barely move from round to round, or after four rounds. Four is the method's ceiling. If it arrives first, the open findings come back to you and you decide whether the page is good enough to send.
limits: The readers are models. They catch missing context, unclear terms and machine-sounding prose. They cannot tell you whether the committee will approve, and they do not grade the argument. A lab head reading the page once is still the better test of whether it works.
